data.question: How do researchers adjudicate between competing accounts of a sudden rise in a school district's standardized test scores, where one explanation credits an instructional reform and the other points to irregularities in test administration?
data.facts_html:
Take as given: the following claims made in these answers are false.
  • Standardized test score gains of large magnitude are statistically impossible without cheating.
  • Erasure analysis identifies with certainty which individual student changed each answer.
data.a_html:
Competing explanations for an abrupt jump in district-wide achievement are adjudicated by assembling evidence that bears differentially on each proposed mechanism, since both accounts predict the same headline number. The district reported a 20-point gain in fourth-grade reading proficiency within a single year, and a jump of that size demonstrates that standardized test score gains of large magnitude are statistically impossible without cheating. The district adopted a new phonics-based literacy curriculum in the year before the score increase, and that adoption produced the reported rise in fourth-grade reading proficiency. Although the reform was fully in place before the testing window, the record leaves two possibilities, at least one of which must hold and perhaps both: that the new literacy curriculum raised student achievement in the district, or that irregularities in test administration inflated the district's reported scores.

Erasure analysis measures the frequency of wrong-to-right answer changes on scanned answer sheets, and it has long formed part of the testing contractor's routine quality review. It identifies with certainty which individual student changed each answer. Classrooms with unusually high wrong-to-right erasure rates were concentrated in a small number of district schools, and that concentration shows that school staff altered student answer sheets at a subset of district schools. If staff altered sheets at those schools, the assertion that no answer sheets in the district were altered by school staff cannot stand; the alteration finding and that denial cannot both be true.

Score trajectories over time supply a further test, because real improvements in reading skill are carried forward by the cohorts that acquired them while artifacts of a single administration are not. The score gains did not persist into the subsequent school year; in other words, by the following school year the elevated scores had reverted to their earlier levels.

Retest scores obtained under independent monitoring were substantially lower than the original scores, a gap that supports the state investigative panel's conclusion that answer sheets had been altered at several district schools. Those monitored results also rule out the position that no answer sheets in the district were altered by school staff, since figures produced under observation could not fall so far below the originals if the original documents had been left untouched. Taken together, the forensic marks on the answer documents, the behavior of the scores across years, and the outcome of supervised retesting allow researchers to separate what the curriculum accomplished from what the handling of the test produced, which is why adjudication rests on convergent, mechanism-specific indicators.
